sections.title: Identification
sections.text: Cortinarius orellanus has a dry, finely felted or slightly scaly tawny to reddish-orange cap, first convex and later flatter, often with a low central bump and an inrolled edge. Its relatively widely spaced, attached gills change from pale yellowish or ochre to rusty red-brown. The fibrous stalk is ochre to orange-brown, often slightly curved and narrowing towards the base. Young specimens may show a delicate yellowish cobweb-like veil, the cortina, between cap and stalk; this usually disappears. The spore print is rust brown. Smell can be radish-like but is not a dependable diagnostic feature.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: It is an ectomycorrhizal woodland fungus, especially with broadleaf trees such as oak, though it can also occur under conifers and on acidic or alkaline soils. In Britain it fruits mainly from late summer through autumn. Local occurrence and season vary. A brown or orange webcap cannot be identified from colour, season or tree association alone.

sections.title: Similar species
sections.text: Many Cortinarius species look similar, including the equally dangerous Cortinarius rubellus. A faint or absent cortina on a mature mushroom does not exclude a webcap. The spaced ochre-to-rust gills and finely felted cap are helpful clues, but expert examination is needed for uncertain specimens.

sections.title: Orellanine poisoning
sections.text: Orellanine can damage kidney tubules after a long symptom-free interval. Digestive symptoms may begin 24–36 hours after a meal or be absent; thirst, dry mouth, flank or back pain and changes in urine output may appear days later. The Belgian Poison Centre describes kidney signs usually after 8–10 days, sometimes up to 17 days; reports describe a broader range. Some patients need dialysis and a minority progress to permanent kidney failure or transplantation. Outcomes differ: in a 12-person French series, seven recovered normal kidney function over 13 years, four received transplants and one remained on dialysis. Suspected ingestion warrants urgent medical assessment before symptoms appear.

traits: Dry finely felted tawny-orange to reddish-brown cap, often with low central bump
Relatively widely spaced attached gills, yellowish ochre becoming rust brown
Fibrous ochre to orange-brown stem, often tapering at its base
Delicate cobweb-like cortina in young specimens, usually fleeting; no persistent ring
Rust-brown spore print; usually with broadleaf trees in late summer to autumn
safetyNote: Potentially deadly kidney poison: never eat Cortinarius orellanus. Orellanine injury may remain silent for days before severe thirst, back pain and kidney failure develop; absence of early symptoms gives no reassurance. Seek urgent poison-centre or emergency advice after any suspected ingestion.
